text_fidelity_a:
Native Union Night Cable - 10ft Ultra-Strong Reinforced [MFi Certified] Durable Lightning to USB-A Charging Cable with Weighted Knot Compatible with for iPhone 14, iPhone 13 and Earlier (Cosmos) There are two of us in the house that use iPhones with the lightning port and as such we do need extra cables. Lightning cables are great but they do have a tendency to break. Also, not all third-party cables are the same and some are not worth the box they ship in. I was anxious to try this cable and I have found it to be a perfectly acceptable replacement for the one that came with my phone. Actually, it’s better.

First things first - it is important to note that this cable is MFI-certified which is actually a big deal. I have worked with cables that are certified and those that are not. Those that carry certification are guaranteed to work properly with your device, while those that are not certified are a roll of the dice. This cable is certified so it means two things you can expect from it: it will allow you to charge your phone without worry, and it will allow you to connect your phone to your computer without complaining about the cable being unauthorized. It just works.

The cable is shielded in a heavy nylon weave and that is a double-edged sword. On one hand it means the cable is very stiff and not very bendy which may or may not be an issue. More importantly, though, it means it is going to last longer than plastic coated cables which tend to flex and break.

The ends are terminated well too, with a hard plastic sleeve at the end of each plug where the cable connects. This spot is where most cables fail, and it is nice to see that some thought was put into reinforcing the cable at this point.

The weighted ball is interesting but to me it gets in the way. It can be slid up and down the cable which has its uses, but it is large enough and bulky enough to be more of a hindrance to me than a help. That said, if you are putting this cable in an area where it will not be moved and you intend to leave it there for the long term, it does prevent tangles and it allows for keeping gently tension on the cable.

Overall, I am pleased with this cable. It’s a lot less expensive than Apple-branded cables and it definitely is more durable and should last a long time.
text_fidelity_b: Native Union Night Cable - 10ft Ultra-Strong Reinforced [MFi Certified] Durable Lightning to USB-A Charging Cable with Weighted Knot Compatible with for iPhone 14, iPhone 13 and Earlier (Cosmos)

text_fidelity_a:
SENTRY V1.0 Dual Mode Call Blocker I've been relying on a cordless phone system with built-in call blocking, but it only stores 30 numbers. That gets filled up in short order, and I delete them and start over. I needed something better.

And this is definitely better. I'm using it with a cable-provided phone line and cordless phone system. And it works. Mostly.

The cool thing about this system is it intercepts everything by default, and announces that if the caller is a telemarketer, to remove us from their call list. It also announces that the caller can press "0" for the call to go through. This eliminates all robocalls, and most other unsolicited calls.

After the phone number is in the device's caller ID memory, you can then whitelist or blacklist it if you choose. Whitelisted numbers go straight through without an announcement and ring the phone normally. Blacklisted numbers are simply blocked. You might hear a partial ring, but that's the end of it.

There are a couple of down sides. When a caller presses "0", only the ringer in the device itself rings. It does not ring the phone system. If you're not near the room where the device is, chances are you won't hear it. So if you're expecting important calls, it's probably best to set the device to "off" when you're not within earshot of it.

And the other is -- and this may be a fault in the particular unit I received -- the "off" position is not always reliable. More than once it has continued to block calls when set to "off." If a really important call is expected, I'll probably just disconnect the unit from the phone system completely.

Other than that, it's effective. It blocks unwanted calls.
text_fidelity_b: SENTRY V1.0 Dual Mode Call Blocker

Perixx Peripro-303MR Trackball, 1.34 Inch Replacement Ball for Perimice and M570, Matte Red I bought this replacement ball for my Logitech MX ERGO, which worked well for me before I accidentally dropped it and subsequently put a pock mark on the original ball. The ERGO still worked but would occasionally get stuck when the support pegs would catch the pock and cause the ball to resist - not enough to really hurt anything but just enough to make digital drawing difficult and just enough to annoy me. This replacement ball has taken care of that for me and has proven to be a worthwhile expense for me.

The ERGO and the M570 have the same size ball, so this ball can be used in either (I was using the ball from my old M570 in the ERGO while I waited for this ball to arrive). Replacement is a 30-second procedure and requires no special tools, though a pencil does make getting the old ball out a lot easier.

There are two different finish types available, glossy and matte. I chose the glossy in red. Operation has been absolutely smooth with no resistance at all and no catches. I haven’t noticed any operational differences between it and the original gray ball that came in my ERGO. And, in my opinion, the dark red of this ball actually looks a little nicer than the original silver ball as well as the blue M570 ball.

This wasn’t an expensive replacement and so far it has worked out very well for me. It has restored operation of my trackball to what it was before I damaged the original ball, which is really all I needed. Based on my experience with it, this is an easy replacement ball to recommend if you need to replace the ball in either a Logitech M570 or an MX ERGO.
text_fidelity_b: Perixx Peripro-303MR Trackball, 1.34 Inch Replacement Ball for Perimice and M570, Matte Red

text_fidelity_a:
D-Link Wireless N300 Mbps Extreme-N Gigabit Router (DIR-655) We are very satisfied with the two DIR-655s that we have (at two sites). They hold up well and cause no problems. They're fast and stable; they run cool and basically require little or no attention.

Two router features that deserve much more discussion than they usually get are the unit's firewall (if any) and its Quality-of-Service (QoS) engine (if any).

o The firewall keeps external probes and hack-attempts out of your network. You'd be amazed how many probes a home or business broadband connection gets every hour from places like China, Eastern Europe and the Middle East. They're looking for ways in so they can infect your machines and steal your information. A router with a good firewall implemented in its firmware is increasingly essential. Firewalls let internal users establish connections with remote machines, not the other way around. And the DIR-655's firewall is excellent, a stateful-packet-inspection implementation that is truly industrial-class. Frankly, I didn't know this when I bought my first unit but was delighted to discover it once I brought it home. Good stuff. And, it's compatible with my company's virtual-private-network (VPN) approaches, which can be a real problem for firewalls to accommodate. My company has used two VPN approaches in the time I've had our DIR-655s, and there have been no issues.

o A good QoS engine prioritizes time-critical Internet traffic such as voice-over-Internet (VoIP). I did not fully appreciate this until we pulled the plug on our landline and implemented "roll-your-own VoIP", saving 90% off our monthly phone costs (see [...] for details). Only a router with good QoS capabilities will allow phone calls to be clear, crisp and smooth in the face of other Internet traffic. And the DIR-655 turns out to have a very good QoS engine. It automatically prioritizes the standard VoIP ports so our phone calls sound as good as a landline even with two teenagers streaming video, cruising Facebook, listening to Pandora, Skyping and FaceTime-ing, etc. Unfortunately, the marketplace is not yet fully aware of the benefits of a good QoS engine in routers, so it's not a given. Even Apple's well-regarded and excellent Time Capsule and Airport/Airport Extreme routers don't have it, for example. But DIR-655 does.

The only issue we've ever experienced with the DIR-655s in our years of usage was once when a cell phone got into a conniption loop that had it disassociate and reassociate with the router over and over and over again, many times per minute. This caused the router to bog down and reboot itself (and who could blame it). The DIR-655's informative logs helped me diagnose what was going on. Eventually the phone got straightened out, and the problem went away.

UPDATE: I can no longer recommend this router. The latest firmware is abysmal and ruins what was formerly a good product.
text_fidelity_b: D-Link Wireless N300 Mbps Extreme-N Gigabit Router (DIR-655)

Mohu Television Antenna Leaf 30 Paper-Thin Indoor HDTV Antenna for Free TV MH-110502 There are so many good reviews here about this antenna, I'll try not to repeat what others have said. I do have a few tips to add,

When setting up your antenna, do yourself a favor and tie a string through the two holes at the top of the antenna. That way you can hang it on one tack/nail as you're searching for the best location. Have extra tacks or nails handy, as they will jump out of your hand and become lost in the carpet (until you find them the next day with a bare foot).

Buy some very small nails. I've discovered that I need to move the antenna around to get reception for some channels. Therefore I have a fair number of nails in the wall that look a little strange. Small nails are less visually distracting. If I get very ambitious, I might even paint them.

This antenna really works best on an exterior wall facing the majority of transmitting antennas you are trying to reach. So if you're working with an interior wall facing the wrong direction, it probably won't work very well.

To up the number of channels you receive, consider buying a signal amplifier (I bought the RCA Digital Amplifier here on Amazon.) They cost about $15. I added 10 additional channels by using one.

Finally, how well these indoor antennas work largely depends on where you live and how close you are to the transmitting antennas. To avoid disappointment, do some research online before purchasing anything.The site that helped me the most was disablemycable.com .
text_fidelity_b: Mohu Television Antenna Leaf 30 Paper-Thin Indoor HDTV Antenna for Free TV MH-110502

text_fidelity_a:
Synsen Replacement Ear Pads Cushion Compatible for Bose QuietComfort QC2,QuietComfort 15 QC15,QuietComfort QC25,QuietComfort 35 QC35,Bose AE2,AE2i,AE2w,SoundTrue, SoundLink (Around-Ear) Headphones I purchased these replacement pads for my Bose QC-15 headphones as the old pads were torn and needed to be replaced. I selected this set of pads based on the positive reviews here on Amazon with the thought that they would be the same as the original pads. While they look the same, they are indeed slightly different.

First things first - these pads are fairly easy to install though they do require a little persistence to get them to snap into place. The earphones themselves have small tabs around the edges designed to snap the pads' bases into place and hold securely, and if the pads are not snapped down they simply will not stay securely. The inner foam and cloth shield that covers the electronics is easy to install but I had trouble with the double-sided tape that holds them in place - the adhesive did not want to release the cover strip and I had real difficulty peeling that strip away without ripping the actual cloth.

Once in place, the phones look exactly like they did when they were new, but I found three differences. First, the phones no longer fit into the case as easily as they once did. Instead of just turning the cups to lay flat and simply putting them in the case, now I have to mess with them slightly to fit into the case properly, though they can be made to fit. More noticeable, though, is that the pads are not as effective as the originals for passive noise canceling. A fan that I have in my office used to be canceled out almost completely with the combination of passive and active noise canceling but is now more audible than when the original pads were in place. I would not say the difference is enough to render the earphones' ability to cancel noise completely compromised, but they are definitely not the same. Finally, these replacement pads are just a little less supple and soft than the original pads. It is not all that noticeable until comparing the original and replacement pads side by side. You have to really be looking closely for the difference to notice it, but it's there.

The difference in noise canceling ability is most noticeable when working in an environment with reverb. I use my phones to monitor sound coming through a professional sound board because these have always done an excellent job of eliminating reverb and leaving just what comes through the sound board. With these new pads in place, I can now hear a lot of reverb, even when I press the phones tight over my ears and have ensured that they completely cover my ears so it's not a gapping issue. The material is different, plain and simple.

These are not bad replacement pads by any means. They are very good, they are comfortable and they do make these phones look brand new again. That said, they were not manufactured by Bose and there are some differences. When considering the cost difference between these and Bose parts, the trade-offs balance out favorably. If you have to have an exact match with the original pads, these are very close but not 100% identical. If you are satisfied with a [roughly] 90%-95% match, these pads work nicely for a lot less than original manufacturer pads.
text_fidelity_b: Synsen Replacement Ear Pads Cushion Compatible for Bose QuietComfort QC2,QuietComfort 15 QC15,QuietComfort QC25,QuietComfort 35 QC35,Bose AE2,AE2i,AE2w,SoundTrue, SoundLink (Around-Ear) Headphones

The machine has to be set on a hard flat service. I tried to just hold it in the air and it would not work. I made one round and then reapplied the solution, then cranked the machine around again.  (It goes slowly). I buffed the DVD with the cloth as directed and played the DVD. It skipped less than before, but was still skipping.  I repeated the entire process again, and now the DVD works perfectly!.  I want to try this on some very scratched  DVDs and see how far I can push it. I would recommend this for mild to moderately scratched DVDs/ CDs at this point. text_fidelity_a: APC UPS 1500VA UPS Battery Backup and Surge Protector, BX1500M Backup Battery Power Supply, AVR, Dataline Protection If you have electronics, you need a ups battery backup. For years, I have used a backup to prevent loss due to power surges. With a backup, if you are in the middle of working on something on your computer (like a thesis), when the power goes out, it gives you enough time to save your work and shut down the computer safely. In our household, we have 2 desktops, 2 laptops, 4 tvs/monitors, xbox one, ps3, speaker systems, digital piano and more. These are very expensive pieces of equipment, especially the piano. We also have all of our cabling in the garage and keep that on a ups battery backup too. The only thing I don't have on a backup, is the gaming computer. Now it is on a backup. Makes life a little less discouraging if you lose a piece of electronics during a power surge. By the way, it is compact, but it is still pretty heavy. It comes with half surge protected outlets and 5 power/surge protected outlets, cable connection in and out, usb protection and data protection.

Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology [[VIDEOID:fab011cbaf4d8ff273fb360a6d075448]] My granddaughter is too young to remember the big bulky Polaroid instant camera, so when I showed her this camera and told her it took instant pictures that she could use as stickers her comment was "AWESOME", and she's dying to get her hands on it. This compact sized 10 megapixel camera offers users the option of printing 2" x 3" photos instantly or adding up to a 32 GB micro SD card in order to store or share images.

The camera is straight forward and simple to use. If you want to take instant photos just load [[ASIN:B00ZSPI3A6 Polaroid 2x3 inch Premium ZINK Photo Paper TWIN PACK (20 Sheets) - Compatible With Polaroid Snap, Z2300, SocialMatic Instant Cameras & Zip Instant Printer]] into the chamber in the back of the camera, remove the magnetic lens cap, and gently press the viewfinder to turn the camera on.

Using the selector wheel at the top left, you can choose to take your photos in color, black & white, or sepia (which is like old time tin type for an antique look). Choose one, and then press the button next to that to select whether you want the photo to have a border or not. You can even press another button on the top to activate a 10 second delay to take selfies, and there's also a "photo booth mode" which takes a series of six quick pictures over the course of 10 seconds that you can set by depressing the shutter for three seconds.

Once you've chosen all of your desired options simply frame your shot in the viewfinder and press the shutter. There's no zoom or available adjustment, the camera automatically focuses and uses flash if needed, and the 2" x 3" print comes out of the side of the camera clear, sharp, and dry to the touch in under a minute. If you have film loaded the camera is going to print photos automatically when you press the shutter, so don't load paper if you prefer to use the micro SD card and not print. The camera has an auto sleep function that will shut it off to save battery power if sufficient times lapses between use, or you can just press the viewfinder back down to shut it off manually.

There are no instructions that comes with the camera, but you can read or print the manual yourself by going to polaroidsnapcamera dot come. You can also find the firmware update there. Be sure to charge the camera fully when you receive it, then insert a Micro SD card and update the firmware before using it. (Available here: http://polaroid.com/products/polaroid-snap-camera) Besides printing paper, you'll definitely want to have a MicroSD card for the camera and a case: [[ASIN:B017A1D6TI Polaroid Neoprene Pouch for The Polaroid Snap Instant Camera (Black)]].

There are several things about this product that could be improved on:
1. No sample printing paper included
2. No picture preview
3. No strap to attach the lens cover to which would help prevent losing it
4. Viewfinder pops open too easily
5. No instruction manual or link mention of the firmware update (or link to it) included with product

Otherwise, the camera is well made and fun to use. I can see where kids would have a lot of fun with this camera, but the photo paper isn't cheap so I may let my granddaughter use some and then just mostly use the Micro SD card. This could also be useful for producing instant photos at special events such as birthday parties, weddings, proms, and for other occasions, and the peel off backing on the photo paper makes it nice for scrap booking.

This instant camera was provided at no cost for my evaluation and review.
text_fidelity_b: Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology

Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) I am a big fan of my kindles. I have the kindle keyboard ereaders 1st and 3rd gen , the 2nd gen Fire 8.9" and last year I bought the 6" Fire. I would not have bought this one except that my 6" Fire has gotten glitchy. I have not had problems with any of my kindles before so I chalked it up to just a bad egg.
I was thinking of replacing it when I found this great deal on the lastest 7" Fire. $100 for a tablet is such a deal. $50 is AMAZING!!
There isn't a huge difference other than this one is a little bigger. It was easy to import everything from my old tablet to my new one. My books, photos, songs, even my book marks from Silk. The set up took minutes.
The home page is different, it looks like the ones on iphones with all the apps on the home page. You can group them into smaller collections, you can also upload your own photo to be the wallpaper. I like this better than the carousel. You can also group your books into collections. There is a button so that you can move between applications without them closing out. It will show all the last places you went so you can pick up where you were and just switch screens. This is my favorite new feature, even more than the change with the home screen.
I'm not super fond of Silk but it is less annoying since they did an upgrade.
I have only had one problem: when I was first setting it up, the screen kept freezing. I rebooted it and I haven't had an issue since.
This is just as fast as my 6" tablet. Battery usage seems the same as well. According to the specs this should be a little slower than the 6" with less battery time but I have not noticed a difference. The plastic back feels only a little less durable than my other kindles but I'm not concerned. I feel like I have gotten quite a deal.
The camera isn't really improved since there isn't a flash and the sound quality is the same as well. Movies look great. I'm really happy that I can add a memory card. Movies, music, and audio books use a lot of memory but now I'll have more memory than I need.
You are getting so much for your money. I've never used other brand tablets, I'm not an Apple user. They may or may not be better but are their prices worth it?
I love Prime access for music and videos and that they can be downloaded.
I'm very happy with my new tablet!

D&O LIGHTING LED Video Light Panel – 180W Bi-Color Studio Lighting for Video Recording Filming with 97+ CRI - Aluminum Construction, Big Heat Sink Fins and On-Light V-Mount Adapter Plate for Battery I work in photo/video for a living, and I can tell you that good LEDs aren't cheap. I have worked with hot tungsten lamps for high output and smaller LEDs for lightweight smaller setups, but LED lights that can compete with the output of Tungstens are pricey.
That being said, this is a FANTASTIC light. It has high output yet has the pros of LED panels such as lower power consumption and heat, as well as being dimmable and color adjustable from the panel or remote control. I had the opportunity to use this for a job yesterday setting up an interview in an office setting. My tungsten bulbs would have been too bright and need gels to match the rest of the office. My other smaller LEDs would have cast smaller spots and we all know a larger light source casts a more pleasing glow. It seemed effortless to get the amount of light we needed in a short time.
HOWEVER, I did find that the mounting point was a little bit difficult to use. There are two bolts to secure it to the stand, and both need to be loosened to mount it properly. It took me a few attempts to get it on the stand, one side felt like I was screwing the bolt the wrong direction most of the time. Meanwhile, the light is large and kept wobbling during this overly complicated procedure. It didn't feel like a premium product during that, which I found odd considering the price point. I have lights that cost about half of this one that felt more premium during mounting. But, that being said, once the lights are up it works a treat!
So, a solid 4 stars from me. Almost 5 if the mounting were easier or the price lower to make up for that. But as a light, it does what it should do and well.
text_fidelity_b: D&O LIGHTING LED Video Light Panel – 180W Bi-Color Studio Lighting for Video Recording Filming with 97+ CRI - Aluminum Construction, Big Heat Sink Fins and On-Light V-Mount Adapter Plate for Battery

Geeni Sentry Wi-Fi Wireless Smart Floodlight Security Camera, 2-Way Audio, Motion Sensor Alarm, Audio Video Recording, Works with Alexa and Hey Google I have had the opportunity to review a few similar products over the last couple years and this new security light by Sentry has some great features that make it a stand out among other security lights.

I found installation straightforward and simple. For those who have trouble connecting to your WiFi, the most common issue is the strength of the different frequencies your router is broadcasting. The easiest way to resolve this is to go into your router settings via your computer and turn off the 5 GHz band during setup. This is necessary sometimes when initially setting up SmartHome products. While some may find this necessary for this product, I did not using my Orbi router system.

The Geeni App is easy to use and makes setup and customization of how the light operates user friendly.

This unit puts out a huge amount of light - 2100 Lumens to be exact while only using 24 watts of power thanks to it utilizing the LED bulbs.

This is the first security bulb I have reviewed that actually has a built in siren. This could be an outstanding feature if needed. Whether utilized to scare off someone attempting to break in to your home or to cause unwanted pests to run the other way - it will work! This siren is effective because it’s loud.

The speaker can also be used for communication purposes. By utilizing a built in microphone you’ll be able to have conversations with those you are viewing through the camera. The speaker and microphone have a surprisingly high clarity. The only thing I found odd with this aspect of this product is this is not a light you’ll want to place at head height as the light is so bright and the camera is really made to provide a wide angle view. Therefore when you speak through the speaker I found people usually look around and can’t figure out the source of the disembodied voice.

After using this product for the last 6 weeks I have found that it performs excellently. By installing a 128GB micro SD card within it, saving videos is easy and I’ve had plenty of time to review the footage. I love that it holds the recording locally so there is no cloud subscription fee required.

This is an excellent security light that will not only light the night when motion is detected, but will record it, alert you, scare the intruder with a siren or allow you to speak to them (or apologize for just scaring them with the siren).

This is an outstanding product that I definitely recommend.
text_fidelity_b: Geeni Sentry Wi-Fi Wireless Smart Floodlight Security Camera, 2-Way Audio, Motion Sensor Alarm, Audio Video Recording, Works with Alexa and Hey Google

Apple Watch Series 7 [GPS + Cellular 45mm] Smart Watch w/Graphite Stainless Steel Case with Midnight Sport Band. Fitness Tracker, Blood Oxygen & ECG Apps, Always-On Retina Display, Water Resistant This is my fourth Apple watch. I’ve purchased the series 0, series 1, 2, two series 4. One stainless, one aluminum. The 4 is such a great watch, I never felt the need to upgrade. I recently paid Apple $ 79 to replace my battery. They actually replaced the watch. I’ve never had a problem with any Apple watch. I purchased the 7, because of a great Amazon price.

Stainless steel vs aluminum. Both are great. I put one bad scratch on my aluminum crystal. It doesn’t affect function, and it only shows when the watch is dark. It happened when my watch hit the rough edge of our granite countertop. My SS has never scratched.

Why spend the extra money to get the stainless? If you want a GPS only model, the SS is $ 300 more than the aluminum. If you want cellular capability, the difference drops to $ 200. Due to health issues, my wife convinced me to get the cellular capability. In an emergency, these will call 911, even when your phone is not around, and even when you don’t subscribe for service. That’s important.

The series 7 has a blood oxygen measurement feature. During Covid, we purchased two different fingertip devices to measure blood oxygen. We were disappointed with both. The watch oxygen measurement works seamlessly. We consider it worth buying for that feature alone.

Summary.

If you want cellular capability, spend the extra $ 200 for SS. If you don’t, buy the aluminum model and save $ 300.
Both are great watches.
text_fidelity_b: Apple Watch Series 7 [GPS + Cellular 45mm] Smart Watch w/Graphite Stainless Steel Case with Midnight Sport Band. Fitness Tracker, Blood Oxygen & ECG Apps, Always-On Retina Display, Water Resistant

text_fidelity_a:
Kensington Wired SlimBlade Trackball Mouse (K72327U), Black I lived and breathed full-sized Kensington trackball mice from about 1987 until my last one stopped functioning and I couldn't find them anymore...probably in the late '90s. Tried some others; all had small, lightweight balls that gave none of the feel and control of Kensinton's...Expert Mouse? Was that what it was called back then too? Because it was the same general design as the current Expert Mouse, but the body was computer-case white.

Anyway, I had several of those (the quality going downhill with each iteration, as I recall) and loved them, and since they disappeared (as far as I could tell), I adapted, first to trackpads, which I've never liked much, and then back to traditional mice which don't give nearly the control of a trackball. Now, at last, it seems Kensington has again begun to produce truly worthwhile trackball mice, and this is one. Oh, it's _so_ good to have one of these again.

I'm doing that thing I hate when other people do it and reviewing the product as soon as I've gotten it up and running, without any kind of experiential history behind my assessment. I'll come back and update this in the future if necessary. But so far: I'm happy, happy, happy to have a real, full-sized Kensington trackball mouse again, with a heavy, substantial ball. There are only two things about this device that I'm not crazy about: In my old Kensington mice, the ball rested on physical rollers and I could give the ball a good spin and it would keep spinning for a second before stopping; it spun much more freely in its cavity than this ball does (so far...maybe that's something that will break in?) [Update: yes, after about three days of use the ball rolls more smoothly and silently than the old one on rollers ever did]. And the other thing is the scrolling mechanism. It's weird. Despite the KensingtonWorks software trying to make us believe otherwise, the "scroll ring" itself actually has nothing to do with scrolling, nor with anything else - the "scroll ring" is not even a control, but just a static piece of chrome trim. What makes the mouse scroll is twisting the ball this way or that from the top, as if it were a knob. At first I thought the "scroll ring" wasn't working because I was trying to use it without touching the ball...which does nothing. And now that I've figured out how scrolling works (you rest your finger on the "scroll ring" and push and pull the side of the ball)...I'm not crazy about it. I'm getting used to it, but it's just a weird way to scroll (I can't for the life of me remember how I used to do it on the Expert Mouse decades ago). It does work though.

(Update on the scrolling: I'm also not crazy about the way the KensingtonWorks software handles the scrolling speed adjustment. When you make the base pointer movement speed faster, the pointer continues to move smoothly, but just faster. When you make the scrolling speed faster though, you lose all smoothness - the software makes the scrolling faster by breaking it into successively larger and more jarring jumps. At the slowest speed, it's pretty smooth; at the highest speeds it's no longer really scrolling, but simply jumping abruptly from one screenful (or page) to the next. Increasing the scrolling speed just increases the size of these jumps, but I find them jarring and annoying starting at the second or third lowest speed setting.)

I also had to figure out how to program one of the buttons as a click lock, since Kensington doesn't call it that anymore, but calls it "left drag", "right drag", and "middle drag" (and I have no idea what the difference is between those three - I just chose "left drag" and it's working fine).

So far, those are my only gripes, all minor. So happy to have one of these things again! =) (Did I mention that?)

Enjoy...
text_fidelity_b: Kensington Wired SlimBlade Trackball Mouse (K72327U), Black

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech 3.5 mm Analog Stereo Headset H151 with Boom Microphone - Black, 7.9"x5.7"x2.4" Good crisp audio quality for phone calls. I like an on-the-ear headset instead of in-ear because cell phones have little or no sidetone.

Don't know what sidetone is? Back in the day, land line phone handsets fed the sound from the mic back into the earpiece, so a person could clearly monitor their own voice (and also hear any other sounds that the other party could hear that the mic picked up). That enabled a person to modulate their own voice (instead of screeching in order to hear themselves) and speak much more clearly. It made for a much better phone conversation experience. That feature was called sidetone.

It's a feature that cell phone designers and engineers somehow decided not to add to cell phones, or to make it so low in volume as to be nonexistent.

So until either cell phone engineers put sidetone back into cell phones or headset manufacturers start building it in as a feature, the workaround is on-ear headsets that allow you to hear your own voice while you speak.

The downside is that on-ear headsets aren't exactly convenient to carry around, and they're not inconspicuous. And they can be a bother if you're wearing a hat.

But they do give you some natural sidetone by allowing you to hear the sound of your voice. And this headset from Logitech, as I said, has some good crisp audio quality for phone calls.

Which brings up another point. Even after years of development, possibly the thing cell phones still do worst is make phone calls. The audio can still be garbled and fluttery due to digitizing and signals that fade in and out in strength. So good audio quality---in that mid-range EQ sweet spot---can make cell phone calls a lot more pleasant.

While there's a volume control on the cord, there's no answer button. That's probably a decision to keep the headset compatible with many devices.

Overall, good headset.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech 3.5 mm Analog Stereo Headset H151 with Boom Microphone - Black, 7.9"x5.7"x2.4"

text_fidelity_a:
TomTom Via 1525SE 5 Inch GPS Navigation Device with Free Traffic, Free Maps of the US, Advanced Lane Guidance and Spoken Turn-By-Turn Directions I was so excited to finally have a separate GPS again, as my Garmin one was from 2009 (OLD maps) and using my phone was unsafe because even with stuff disabled during driving, I was still getting messages and interruptions that would pop up, plus I like listening to something on the drive, and using it as a GPS makes that tricky. Having tried several Garmin models, Apple Maps, and Google Maps, I was excited to try TomTom. And I was disappointed.

Problems:
•Screen is VERY dim in the sunlight, and living in Florida, this is most of the time. It is NOT easy to see the map, which even in my ancient Garmin is much more visible and automatically switches from day mode to night mode. Likewise, my iPhone screen automatically changes brightness for the amount of sun coming in. And this? It looks horribly dim and takes a lot of effort to see.
•Routes don’t always make sense. I’m used to some amount of this in the other systems I’ve tried, but they’re really wacky on this thing, taking a REALLY scenic route that sometimes involves making a full circle for something that was literally as easy as just turning left in the correct place.
•Point of interest search is slow and ineffective. Even with my ancient Garmin (and obviously with my phone), it would never find most places, even ones that have been there many years. This after waiting an interminable amount of time for the list to compile. Did I get the long update on my computer and add it to the GPS? Yep. I thought that was the problem, did the update, and then discovered it was Not the problem.
•Doesn’t appear to take traffic into account. Neither does my old Garmin, but it should do better than a piece of tech that’s 10 years old and at least be comparable to a current smartphone’s GPS; otherwise, what’s the point?
•Hard to stop. You want to sometimes say, “OK SHUT UP. I know the rest of the way!”, and in all other GPS systems I’ve tried, getting to the “end route/stop” place is usually two steps, max. It is long and complicated, and I don’t want to die in a car accident, so I end up having to suffer through unnecessary and often over-complicated routes that make no sense.
•Doesn’t default to turn-by-turn. Sometimes it shows an aerial view, which is zero helpful, has no detail, and requires me to think a lot about “is this to MY right or left if my car is facing this way and the map is oriented North Up and I *think* I am moving East maybe, but I can’t tell because this stupid thing is both dim and also has an unbelievably zoomed out map view where I’m not sure Where my little dot is going?!?!”

So yes. Unless I sit in the parking lot and fiddle with it for a good while, nothing is quite right, and everything takes a long time to find or set up. I tried it for a month now, and my opinion has not changed. This is frustrating.

Good things:
•nice size screen
•fun voices

Overall rating: 2 stars. I like Garmin more, and I am quite unhappy with this. It is slightly better than my now failing 10-year-old Garmin GPS. *slightly*. I would not buy this or recommend it. The interface is cumbersome, the visibility is bad in the sun, and finding places is a pain and basically 100% of the time requires me to just search for an address on my phone and plug it in. Nope.
text_fidelity_b: TomTom Via 1525SE 5 Inch GPS Navigation Device with Free Traffic, Free Maps of the US, Advanced Lane Guidance and Spoken Turn-By-Turn Directions

text_fidelity_a:
VELCRO Brand ONE-WRAP Cable Ties, 100Pk, 8 x 1/2" Black Cord Organization Straps, Thin Pre-Cut Design, Wire Management for Organizing Home, Office and Data Centers I use these exclusively for cable management - I pass the end of the strap through the slot so that the strap is permanently secured to the cable, then bundle the cord up. EZPZ. Great value for the money, I bought two bags to organize my cables and I should probably be set for the next twenty years or so. Much better than constantly scavenging velcro straps from new purchases. I prefer these to wire ties, as they can be secured to the cable, stick better, apply force over a broader area and look a far bit more orderly when properly installed.

The straps are of good quality, adhere very well, and are easy to remove when you want to. The length is suited for wrapping up, say, most of your average 10-15ft computer or AV cables, it hasn't been a problem yet.

Only annoying thing is that when the factory punched out the slots in the strap, it only did so partially, so the little central bit is still stuck to the velcro most of the time. Bothersome, but not excessive so, you just have to tear it off each time. Another nitpick would be that I prefer my straps to have a constant width, rather than tapering down near the end - again, looks neater IHMO.

Other than that, would recommend.
text_fidelity_b: VELCRO Brand ONE-WRAP Cable Ties, 100Pk, 8 x 1/2" Black Cord Organization Straps, Thin Pre-Cut Design, Wire Management for Organizing Home, Office and Data Centers

text_fidelity_a:
ASUS WiFi Gaming Router (RT-AC5300) - Tri-Band Gigabit Wireless Internet Router, Gaming & Streaming, AiMesh Compatible, Included Lifetime Internet Security, Adaptive QoS, Parental Control, MU-MIMO Edit: 12-27-2017
Still very much liking my purchase. Still rocking Merlin firmware. No issues with stability or performance.

Edit:

I have moved from the standard firmware to an open version, search for "ASUSWRT-Merlin" if interested. This has fixed my IP address issue as well as made several other improvements. The changes are too many to mention. That doesn't mean new features but bug fix's and so forth. However, if non stock firmware is not your cup of tea. ASUS rolls many of the fixs into its firmware from my understanding. So if you want to maintain more stock and less bleeding edge. Simply wait a bit longer and most of the changes will make it to you.

I am still very thrilled with my purchase.

The only thing I find meh is the antennas tend to be more floppy than I would like. However if you set it and don't get behind it monkeying around they stay just fine. I am sure many of us know the cord hell behind the entertainment center. This past go round I eliminated 90% of that and hopefully made it future proof. The only area still needing tweaking is behind my router. :(

Oh, I also turned off the smart connect feature. I was having issues with some of my iOS devices and its just easier for me to keep 3 separate SSID's and use them.
I maintain the following.
1 - 2.4 GHz for the IOT devices such as smart lights switches, older iOS devices of the kid's, etc.
1 - 5 GHz for all higher capable devices, media streaming devices so forth. Also configured as failover protection in devices that can support multiple configs and use ethernet first and wifi on failure of ethernet.
1 - 5 GHz for the wife's MacBook / iOS devices, my MacBook / iOS devices etc.

I am going to experiment using the smart connect more soon and see if the previous usage changes.

Original:
I purchased this to replace an aging Airport Extreme. I love the unit. It is easy to setup and the GUI is stable in Safari on OSX, Which I, often find other manufacturers have issues with. I had returned a competing product a week earlier as it had a security flaw. I could not be happier with my decision to spend the extra money. I generally believe you get what you pay for however, I was skeptical. So far it lives up to expectations and I think I received my moneys worth. It is a hefty sized unit. As for range, I have an older plaster walled home ( @ 1300 sq f) with metal mesh backing through out the home. Normally router signal don't play well, however the unit appears to reach all the corners of my home. I was using multiple Airport expresses as access point to fill in the holes so to speak. I have been able to turn off those units.

The only issue I had with the unit is the static IP is capped at 64 places. Additionally the GUI will take mac addresses as lower case. *Do not input the addresses using lower case.* It will prevent you from customizing the device name and the graphic. Once you remove the entry and re add it properly using upper case letters/numbers, you can easily customize the entry to your liking. This small issue is by no means a deal breaker for me. Its good points far out weigh its few issues.
text_fidelity_b: ASUS WiFi Gaming Router (RT-AC5300) - Tri-Band Gigabit Wireless Internet Router, Gaming & Streaming, AiMesh Compatible, Included Lifetime Internet Security, Adaptive QoS, Parental Control, MU-MIMO

I do a Jessica Smith DVD - 10K Walking Workout (see link on bottom of this review) and Leslie Sansone ("Walk at Home"). However, ONE is super accurate on my walks outside and around the office. My bottom line is 10K steps a day but I tend to walk 17K a day. I worked my way up to this since October 2015. I have a sedentary job so walking happens 3 to 4 times a day with a minimum of a mile on each walk. Yes, I have lost weight, @ 40 lbs. There is at least that much more that needs to be lost as well. Hair color is silver if that helps you define the situation.

I love the little activity record feature and use it often (hold down the button to start and hold it down to end when activity is over). This is great when competing with friends where a challenge is inevitable. Speaking of friends. YEAH! That is where the FITBITs excel. I have a few friends in my community now and I love keeping up with them. Motivation features are fantastic!

This little baby doesn't buzz, which also means that the battery life is HUGE!! I think it goes 7 to 8 days before I need to be charged up. I tend to let it go dead because it warns you it needs to be charged about 1 1/2 days before it really does. I've only charged mine 3x now. It takes about an hour to charge. I wait until the visible battery = FULL!

This sweet little tracker is awesome! I started test driving the flex before getting the ONE which I also enjoyed but not as much as this one. I will buy the HR when this ONE dies or I just feel like bringing home another one. The reason I like this one better than the flex is because I don't tend to be an arm swinger and for me this one seems to work better (walking while pushing a cart). The best thing about the arm band models is that you affix it and forget it (until charging time) for which you should get a phone alert.

I don't bother with the sleep feature because I have an app (Sleep Cycle Alarm) on the phone that I use for which I love the beautiful melodious wake up sound. However the ONE comes with a little band for you to slide the ONE into obtain the reading for sleep.

Tripp Lite USB C to HDMI Multiport Video Adapter Converter 4K w/ USB-A Hub, USB-C PD Charging Port & Gigabit Ethernet Port, Thunderbolt 3 Compatible, USB Type C, USB Type-C (U444-06N-H4GU-C),White Update: I corrected this review, since it seems that the HDMI not working is a limitation on my Asus computer (the USB-C device doesn't support the HDMI video transmission, and apparently Asus has no plans to update).

I needed this adapter for my new Asus laptop (Win10), which came without an ethernet port or an hdmi port. The ethernet connection worked really well, I was getting full gigabit connectivity, with no detectable difference from a direct RJ45 connection.

The USB3 worked very well too: I hooked up an external SSD and was able to get high speed file transfers without any problems.

However, I was not able to get the HDMI connector to work at all. I looked for a missing driver on the TrippLite website, but didn't find anything. Without that, the device just didn't detect the monitor plugged into the HDMI port. Just to make sure, I tested the setup using another computer, and everything worked immediately, so I though the problem was this adapter. Turns out that it's actually a limitation on my Asus laptop's USB-C port. I fault TrippLite for making this a bit obscure and not being clear about the requirements, but that's all.

I did not test the charge port.

Given that an important feature doesn't work, I can't justify giving this adapter more than 3 stars. It's excellent (5 stars) for the two ports that I used and did work.
text_fidelity_b: Tripp Lite USB C to HDMI Multiport Video Adapter Converter 4K w/ USB-A Hub, USB-C PD Charging Port & Gigabit Ethernet Port, Thunderbolt 3 Compatible, USB Type C, USB Type-C (U444-06N-H4GU-C),White

Unfortunately, although providing a cleaner looking profile, I began to experience connectivity issues. The streaming became very laggy and would totally lose signal on several occasions. At first, I blamed my internet provider and location of my router but after testing the systems speed as well as relocating the hardware for "better and uninterrupted" service I CONTINUED to have issues. After some more troubleshooting I finally, as a hail mary pass, tried reinstalling the original power hook up and low and behold I have had ZERO problems since. I really wish that I could have had the cleaner no cable look but I'd rather deal with that problem and have to hide an extra cable than be continually concerned that at any moment the show I'm watching will cut off and not be able to restart. text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm Instax Mini 26 + Rainbow Film Bundle - Black A long time ago I had access to a Polaroid Instamatic camera. It was great - snap a picture, it spits out a sheet. Wait about 2 minutes and what you have is a printed photograph. Polaroid is gone now (though the name gets licensed over and over again), and with it went all of the film for the camera that made it so useful. This new camera by Fuji brings back some of the fun of instant photos, though it is by no means perfect and it suffers from some of the same issues the older Polaroid camera had.

The idea is very straightforward - point-and-shoot, and the camera ejects an exposure that will develop over a few moments and will be fully developed in approximately 2 minutes. This is great for social events and is a fun way to share candid shots. The camera is very lightweight and it is small too so it is easy to pack and carry with you.

There are a few issues with the camera, though, some of which are very much like the old Polaroids of days gone by. The images do come out a bit grainy and are definitely not high resolution. If you are looking for images with nice, clean edge detail and bright, vibrant colors, this is going to disappoint you. Also, the images are really small, a little bigger than a passport picture but not by very much. And finally, the film is relatively expensive, a pack of exposures coming with only 10 slides and costing about $0.60 per exposure.

On the plus side, the camera is very easy to use and the camera body itself is not very expensive at all.

There are trade-offs with this camera. On one hand, it is super convenient, it’s fun and it’s relatively inexpensive. However, exposure quality is mediocre, pictures are small and on a per-picture basis the exposures are somewhat expensive. To me, the fun factor weighs heavily in favor of this camera and offsets some of the negatives. For social gatherings and recreational events, this is a fun camera and will serve well. Do not expect to have high-end results, though.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm Instax Mini 26 + Rainbow Film Bundle - Black

text_fidelity_a:
XBOOM Mini Portable Capsule Speaker with Rechargeable Battery and Enhanced Bass+ Resonator (Mini - Black) -1 pack I've been using an Altec Lansing iM227 (a model that is no longer produced by Altec Lansing, but comparable models are still offered) for a couple of years and have been very pleased with it. The Xboom, however, gives me much the same performance at half the size.

The sound quality of the Xboom is impressive for the size. It puts out nearly the same bass level as the iM227, which is surprising given how small it is. It does suffer a bit in the mid and upper ranges, which do not come through as clearly and sharply as the iM227. But the output is more than adequate for enjoyment.

I really like how the two halves of the speaker can be closed up and turned into a small ball that is only about 2 inches tall. Very compact so it easily fits into a bag or jacket pocket - this speaker is designed to be carried around easily. It comes with a decent cloth pouch plus a USB charge cable.

While it will work when it is in its compact mode, for best sound it needs to be unlatched so it expands to about 3 inches tall.

Unlike the iM227 it has an internal battery (the iM227 runs on 3 AAA batteries). That's both good and bad: good for ease of use and compact size; bad in case the internal battery fails, which renders the speaker useless. The Xboom has a stated run time of "up to 12 hours" according to the specs, which is pretty accurate - I got about 10 hours out of a fresh battery. Recharge time is about 2 hours.

Operation is very simple: plug in the attached cable to your device (I'm using it as a speaker for a small mp3 player), turn it on, and listen. The Xboom has a volume control, which the iM227 lacks, and an on/off switch. There's a power indicator light on the bottom of the speaker.

Unlike the iM227, the Xboom can be daisy-chained to other Xbooms for a bigger sound. I only have one, so I can't say how well that works, but it's a nice feature.

Complaints are virtually nil. If I had to come up with something, I'd say that it would be nice to have the power indicator light on the top rather than the bottom so it would be more easily visible as a reminder to power down and save battery life. Minor point, however.

While the sound quality of the Altec Lansing is better, the size and convenience of the Xboom makes it the one I'll take along with me and use more often. Very good value for the price, and I would highly recommend it.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: XBOOM Mini Portable Capsule Speaker with Rechargeable Battery and Enhanced Bass+ Resonator (Mini - Black) -1 pack

text_fidelity_a:
APLOS Industrial Mini PC Powerful Intel Core i5-7267U Max Turbo Frequency 3.5Ghz Fanless Desktop Computer, 8GB RAM 256GB SSD WIN10 Pro OS, 6 x Gigabit Ethernet Network Firewall Gateway Router This is a very cool piece of computing hardware for specific uses. The fanless design means unlike other mini PCs that I've tried, this is actually silent! I'm surprised because the i5 CPU should generate more heat than the miserly Celeron that other mini PCs use, but the fins seems to dissipate heat rather well so far.
The 6 ethernet ports means this can make a pretty cool Windows-powered server for internet or file serving, and the fanless design means it can sit in a home users' closet and not make any audible noise either! While the CPU is pretty good, the GPU is pretty...not. If you look at the attached user benchmark, you'll see the CPU benched at about 74th percentile, but the GPU at a disappointing 4th percentile.
That means you won't really use this for things like games, not that anyone was expecting to. However, it does sort of limit this use for something like a media server using a platform such as Plex, as it would rely on the GPU for real-time media encoding.
For just playing back HD video it should be sufficient, and for other kinds of custom home server use and/or industrial use, this is a pretty interesting and useful product!
text_fidelity_b: APLOS Industrial Mini PC Powerful Intel Core i5-7267U Max Turbo Frequency 3.5Ghz Fanless Desktop Computer, 8GB RAM 256GB SSD WIN10 Pro OS, 6 x Gigabit Ethernet Network Firewall Gateway Router

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Evolve 65e Wireless Neckband Headset, Link 370, MS-Optimized – Bluetooth Headset with up to 13 Hours of Battery Life – Superior Sound for Calls and Music – Passive Noise Cancelling Headset I ordered the 'Jabra Evolve 65e UC & Link 370 Wireless Professional Earbuds' as I'm a sucker for trying out new wireless earbuds. I've tried various different types. Some that are "truly wireless", some like these that have the connected wire around the neck. These Jabra Evolve 65e earbuds are really pretty amazing for what they are. Sound is great but not booming with bass. They are crisp yet not loud. There is really no sound isolation as the buds don't fit snug in the ear, (even trying the included different size tips and wings) but that seems to be on purpose. As from I can tell from reading about these, is that they are meant to allow some outside sound, so that if you are say jogging, you should be able to hear to be safe right? Now with that said, I see the purpose and the market for these earbuds, and there is absolute value to these.
Pairing these to my Android mobile phone was an absolute breeze. Also, using the USB Bluetooth adapter on my Chromebook made pairing these super simple as well.
Call quality is on par with most wireless earbuds. It's good, but not the same as just using your phone obviously but better than some "cheap" buds I've tried. These are definitely built with the Jabra quality you would expect and I'm overall impressed.
They fit comfortably and secure and I've had no issue with them popping out, but then again I'm not a jogger. They are easy to fit into your ears, unlike others that I've had that take a bit of twisting to get the fit just right.
The app is nice and works well but as with most apps like this, it's gimmicky. I mean I've played with it a bit at first but any more, I just pop the buds in and go, and haven't used the app in quite a while.
So to summarize, these are great earbuds if you don't need "truly wireless" and you don't need sound isolation.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra Evolve 65e Wireless Neckband Headset, Link 370, MS-Optimized – Bluetooth Headset with up to 13 Hours of Battery Life – Superior Sound for Calls and Music – Passive Noise Cancelling Headset

Amazon Kindle Fire HDX 8.9" Standing Leather Origami Case (will only fit Kindle Fire HDX 8.9" - 3rd Generation), Red I had the very first kindle...with a red leather first gen case. I was really excited to get the new hdx 8.9" kindle and a new red leather case. These origami cases seem like a good idea. But if you have them sitting on any kind of slightly slick surface or slightly inclined surface, it won't stand up. The function of the "origami" part is a little complicated, but the pictures help. Initially it is it very stiff and hard to "fold". After a few uses it loosens up which makes setting up the "standing" position a little easier, but it still resists the action and as I mentioned, slips. I was thinking a little rubber edge all around the case edge would help some. The case "attaches" to the kindle via magnets and turns your kindle on automatically when you open the case, off when up close it. On the up side, I definitely prefer the feel of the leather case as opposed to the plastic one. Sadly neither case really functions as it should for standing. However it will provide some protection for the glass which is a pretty good size now. In addition to the magnet set in, there is are outer power and volume buttons. They are in good locations and I have not hit them accidently. In fact those buttons are quite handy.
I just wish they'd put more thought into actual function and less into "wow this looks cool" on the stand part.
Hope this helps some. I have not found a great alternative yet, but I will keep looking and update this review if I find one.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Kindle Fire HDX 8.9" Standing Leather Origami Case (will only fit Kindle Fire HDX 8.9" - 3rd Generation), Red

Garmin vívofit 2 Activity Tracker, White The circumference of my wrist is 5 1/4 inches above the bone which is fairly small and the small wristband fits perfectly, there are still 5 holes (1.5 inches) left to make it smaller.

The two reasons I went for this activity tracker are it is waterproof and the battery lasts one year... for me these are the most important reasons because I really hate all this constant charging of gadgets.

Syncing is easy, at the end of the day I just press one button and it syncs with my smartphone, it also comes with a little blue-tooth USB attachment if you want to sync it with your computer. I've read they will add autosync with the next software update which is supposed to arrive shortly.

You get to choose what to see on your screen when you press the button, I went with steps, goal, distance and time. You can also add the date, calories and heart rate if you are wearing a strap.

I absolutely love how it feels, it doesn't bother me at all, you don't have to wear it real tight and the silicon is very soft.

The reason I took one star off is that the beep sound which comes on after one hour of inactivity (when the red warning line appears) is way, way, way too quiet. I set an alarm just to check on the beep sound and it was so short and subtle, if there would be any kind of background noise you won't be able to hear it at all.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin vívofit 2 Activity Tracker, White

Kindle Paperwhite 3G, 6" High Resolution Display with Built-in Light, Free 3G + Wi-Fi - Includes Special Offers [Previous Generation - 5th] My title pretty much sums it up - I love the Kindle Paperwhite! I am a big reader, but I resisted the e-reader obsession until December 2010 when I gave into a Nook. Back then I decided on a Nook because the Kindle did not allow you to borrow books from the library, which was a deal breaker for me.

Fast-forward two and a half years... My Nook was getting older and the discrepancy between prices and availability of e-books between Amazon and Barnes & Noble was becoming increasingly clearer. Also, I love Amazon as a general rule, and order from them pretty heavily for a variety of items, so it made sense to switch over. After brief research, I stumbled upon the Kindle Paperwhite. It met all of my requirements - a dedicated e-reader (no tablet for me, thanks), with a built in light. Yippee! My hubby and puppy (okay, just the hubby) purchased the Kindle Paperwhite for my birthday at the end of August and it was love at first sight. It is unreasonable to compare the Kindle Paperwhite to my old Nook, so I won't. I can freely admit that most of my love comes from the new technology and association with Amazon. I love the light. It is awesome to not have to use a clip on light at night. They are usually terrible and not evenly spaced. The light makes reading at night a breeze. Plus, it is a perfect light, so it really is like reading a book and not like reading on a backlit screen (a la the iPhone or iPad). I love the ease of purchasing books from Amazon, and I love their prices and special deals. But, most of all, I love checking out library books! The very thing that turned me away from the Kindle initially is now the best. There is no need to connect my Kindle to a laptop to download a book. Yay! I can just wirelessly send a book to my Kindle, the same as purchasing one. You must be a wireless network (not 3G), but that my dear friends is a tiny issue. Overall, I love my Kindle Paperwhite and I cannot think of one single thing to make it better! Love it.

Helpful tips - 3G or not? I love the 3G, but it's not a necessity if you have wide access to wireless. I would definitely say to go for the ads, however. They are entirely inoffensive and unobtrusive. They only come up when your Kindle is asleep. Save the $20 and buy yourself a few books!
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Paperwhite 3G, 6" High Resolution Display with Built-in Light, Free 3G + Wi-Fi - Includes Special Offers [Previous Generation - 5th]

text_fidelity_a:
EarStudio ES100 MK2-24bit Portable High-Resolution Bluetooth Receiver/USB DAC/Headphone Amp with LDAC, aptX HD, aptX, AAC (3.5mm Unbalanced & 2.5mm Balanced Output) Very nice features, sounds great, 2.5 balanced output! BT v5, aptXHD, top of the line DAC’s, great battery life. So why just 4 stars? The documentation leaves a lot to be desired. The included printed doc was about the size of a matchbook with writing so small it required a magnifying glass to read and for all that effort it basically said nothing. The biggest hassle was the pairing. It couldn’t be less intuitive. I have many BT devices, both receivers and transmitters and this is the first one that required a web search to figure out. Very frustrating. And to enable the BT v5 it requires a ROM flash upgrade so you have to connect it to a PC and follow a bunch of steps that are as intuitive as the pairing. I came within seconds of sending it back but stuck it out because it had some pretty stellar reviews. It turns out I’m glad I did. Once you get it sorted out it is a pretty amazing piece of kit. I use it with my HiBy r6 and BGVP DMG’S as well as my ATH M-50x headphones. I can now roam freely around the kitchen while keeping the DAP safely out of the way. I can plug-in the 2.5mm balanced cable and get outstanding sound with the added bonus of not heating up the DAP (it gets hot when plugged in directly) and the battery life of the HiBy is more than doubled. Both of these bonuses more than make up for the minor degradation in sound staging. I have listened for over 7 hours without the battery giving up, but have not used it up to it’s limit yet so I can’t say how long it will last. Is it worth the Benjamin it cost? Oh yeah.

Update: Upgraded to 5 stars after a month of use. Once the niggling little details were figured out and the unit was set up I can't say enough good things about this puppy. My main reason for getting a BT transmitter was I am going to be doing extensive bicycle touring later this year and since it will be solo touring I wanted good quality music available. I have an extensive library of 24 bit flac's as well as a couple of hundred audiobooks for the trip and while the playback of the books isn't important the music is. I invested a fair amount of cash into a HiBy R6 DAP and BGVP DMG IEM's as well as upgraded cables to connect them. The EarStudio lets me connect via 2.5" balanced with no real discernible degredation in the quality of the playback as opposed to plugging directly into the output on the DAP, and here's the kicker, instead of just getting 6 - 7 hours of playback and heating up the DAP I now get double that without any heat. I can stash the HiBy in a Pelican 1020 case and put it in my top tube bag where it's out of harms way and protected in case of misadventure. The EarStudio has a battery life of around 14 hours (I haven't run it out yet, and I have listened for over 8 hours). Added to that the App that is available for my Android based DAP is amazing. More fiddly bits than your above average geek could ever want. So I gotta give it a 5 star rating. And it's worth twicw the price but don't tell Radsone.
text_fidelity_b: EarStudio ES100 MK2-24bit Portable High-Resolution Bluetooth Receiver/USB DAC/Headphone Amp with LDAC, aptX HD, aptX, AAC (3.5mm Unbalanced & 2.5mm Balanced Output)

text_fidelity_a:
Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology This is a cameras that is perfect for some but not something that everyone will find useful. The ideal user is someone who wants a simple to use digital camera that has the ability to instantly print the photo without dealing with a PC or conventional printer. This does a pretty good job of accomplishing that goal. But, if you’re looking for a more advanced point and shoot with lots of image features, this may not be your best option.

The camera itself feels very solid, but lacks a key digital camera feature: a view screen. At first glance may seem to be a major omission. But, this camera is designed to be a high-tech replacement for the old-style Polaroid instant cameras by instantly (well, relatively instantly) printing the photo on Zink paper. Note that the paper needs to be purchased separately, and is pretty much an essential component for using the camera. While you can store photos on an SD card, the camera is really designed to be used with the Zink paper.

Usage is very straightforward – it’s about as point and shoot as you can get. That’s great for those who don’t want to fiddle with any settings, but it does put some constraints on image quality. I’ve had about 20% of my photos so far turn out less than ideal due to improper focus, poor white balance, poor resolution and/or incorrect color registration. That’s my major complaint with this camera – the paper is costly, and when you have to toss (or at least not really like) one in five photos, the cost can add up.

The images are small – the paper is only 2 by 3 inches. On the plus side it has a peel and stick backing, so you can use the photos as “post-its” very easily. Again, this is keeping with the intent of the camera, so I won’t downgrade the rating due to the small photo size.

Other negatives for me is that the battery is not user-replaceable. I’ve had too many electronic products with built-in batteries that had to be trashed since the internal battery no longer held a charge. I’m also not fond of the lens cap. It’s very easy to take off (it’s held in place by magnets) but there’s no attachment to the camera, so it’s very easy to misplace.

But this does score well with regard to ease of use and fun. As a test of ease of use I handed this to my Mom who is technically challenged, to say the least. She had no problems snapping photos and loved having the image print right there. She’s never liked using a digital camera in the past due to difficulty using it and dealing with image files. This was right up her ally.

While I’ll drop the rating to 4 stars due to the image quality issues that can crop up, overall this is a unique camera. It’s not right for everyone, but if you’re looking to revisit the days of the Polaroid instant camera while staying in the digital world, this is well worth considering.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology

text_fidelity_a:
Asus Nexus 7 2B32 7-Inch 32 GB Tablet, Black (2013 Model) 7 May 2014: Thanks to Google's omission of full USB OTG function, file transfers are frustrating & sometimes impossible. When I return home, I'm rooting it.

After 24 hours, I like it. It's a little different from my Galaxy Player 5 inch. The extra processor speed is nice. So is the combination of the light weight and larger screen. The GP5 was getting bogged down by software bloat. It fits nicely in my old K3 case. So far, so good.

...and it works with my Targus Bluetooth keyboard. Actually, it works better than it does with the GP5. The Samsung has some key-mapping problems, probably due to Gingerbread.

As to reading, I happened to be starting a novel the other day, and started it on the Nexus 7. I had no problem. I did keep the brightness on 'Auto', so the light level of the screen matched the ambient light. With the GP5, matching light levels was a little chancy, so I had a bit more eyestrain. (Of course the extra 2" of screen have no bearing on that, right?)

I did try the freebie 'La Luna' video that Google gives away. It watched fine on the 7" screen. The thing I really like is that there is a 7" screen in the weight of a past-technology 5" package. I owned a Nook color for 13 days, but took it back because of the weight and balance. It just wasn't comfortable to hold.

I haven't tried any significant music listening. I suspect I'll still prefer my Clip+ for that. The Nexus is a little large for that purpose. I also haven't tried the camera in any particular serious way. A selfie and a picture of my cat isn't much of a trial. Again, I'll probably use a purpose-made camera for real pictures. I also haven't explored portability yet. In the case, it's a bit bulky for easy transport, whereas the GP5 fits in my pocket next to my cell phone. I probably won't put the N7 in my pocket without a case. It's a little large and fragile seeming for that.

...As to the camera, it's OK, the image quality is fine, but a 7" tablet just isn't a good ergonomic platform for picture taking. This is the best from an afternoon at Mass Audubon's Ipswich River Wildlife Sanctuary.

Picture is available at:
MobileRead Forums > E-Book Readers > Android Devices>Nexus 7 2013 1st Impressions

...And I still prefer my Clip+ for music. I hand to hunt around the Android store for a decent player for my collection which includes WMAs as well as MP3s. Google does not play WMAs (cue prissy, superior sniff). I settled on Poweramp, not because it was perfect, but because it was the first one I came to that was good enough. I just want to listen to some music, people, not commit my soul to a single, ringing, crystalline-pure music player that rules them all. Sheesh.

Someday I may do a better review, too. All of the usual things about tablets are at worst adequate on the N7.

Oh, one piece of free advice, worth every penny you paid: Don't go hog wild buying really great accessories. Shop around. A $3 wire easel from a craft store will make a fine desk stand. I have one at work and one at home. A chopstick and a binder clip will do in a pinch. Also, there are good $10 EVA zip cases that will protect your N7 for transport. They don't have to be purpose built. My old K3 had a case that loosely fits the N7 (freebie!) and my KPW1 lives in a similar case. As to ear buds, the candy-colored $5 ones in the bin at the cash register at WalGreens are my favorite, and you never misplace them, because candy-colored.
text_fidelity_b: Asus Nexus 7 2B32 7-Inch 32 GB Tablet, Black (2013 Model)

Kindle, 3G, Graphite, 6" Display with New E Ink Pearl Technology,-R I got the Kindle "keyboard" for my birthday two years ago, and I love it. I have always loved my hard copies of books, but the Kindle is wonderful to travel with. I typically need more than one book with me on a vacation, and I can carry a library around in one slim device. Some of the features that I love:
It is easy to read and operate.
The 3G. It's worth the extra money because there isn't always wifi. You can download a book on the beach if there's enough service (usually there is everywhere).
The battery can last for weeks on end if the wifi/3G is turned off.
The built-in dictionary is handy.
Kindle book prices are typically cheaper than in-store prices, and there are a lot of cheap (< $5) and free books available as well.
Problems I have encountered:
The battery will eventually drain even if you don't use it. If I pick it up after a month of reading paperbacks, it is completely dead.
The screen has broke, twice. I'm not sure if it's just my bad luck, but just after one year of lovingly using my Kindle, the screen froze and refused to work. The one-year warranty was no good (of course), so I had to pay around $80 for a replacement, which also promptly broke 2 weeks later with the same problem. I considered buying a newer model, but they sent me another one free of charge, and that has worked ever since for the past year and a half now. It was worth the hassle and all of my content was saved and easy to retrieve.
Other than that, it is definitely one of my favorite gadgets. I read a lot and this has facilitated my habit of carrying around books everywhere I go.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle, 3G, Graphite, 6" Display with New E Ink Pearl Technology,-R

text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz R3 Dual Dynamic Driver Earphones (V2) I use earbuds a lot since I typically prefer the lightness and ease of use compared with traditional headphones. Right out of the box these were a bit puzzling as to how to position them for use. But, after a bit of fiddling with the over-the-ear loop, it becomes clear.

The in-ear comfort is good. It comes with a variety of ear tips including two types I’ve not used before: a double flange silicon tip and a triple flange silicon tip. The flanges allow the ear bud to make a much better seal in your ear canal. That not only helps cut out ambient noise intruding, it also improves the bass response. I found the double flange works best for me, but the variety of tips included appears sufficient to fit pretty much any ear.

It also comes with an excellent case for storage, and adapters for airplane use and for 1/4 inch plugs. I especially like the case since it’s small enough to make it easy to carry along (roughly 3.5 inches by 3 by 1.5 inches thick) and is reinforced to avoid being crushed. It has mesh pockets to keep everything stowed, and looks nice to boot (black with red contrast in the middle). All-in-all, it’s a great kit in terms of useful accessories.

I’m not as pleased with the cord. While I like how sturdy it is, it has a “Y” link that always seems to be in the way when I’m working out. I got used to it eventually, but a more streamlined cord system would have been a better design approach. Another negative is the 3.5mm plug. It needs to be seated just so or you get sound cut-outs or static. I tried it with several devices to be sure the issue is with the plug and not the device. A more robust plug is needed for this – you shouldn’t have to fiddle with it to get it to seat properly.

The over-the-ear loops are also a bit annoying at first. Granted, that’s certainly due to the fact that I usually use standard in-ear buds without the loop, so any type of loop feels weird to me at first. The material is soft and bendy, so you can position it in any variety of ways. It could benefit from some additional padding. On the plus side, they do hold the buds in very well. Quick head movements that would have loosened an in-ear bud didn’t jar these loose at all.

Now for the really important feature: how they sound. In a word, excellent. My benchmark for moderately-priced earbuds has been units made by RHA out of the UK. These sound nearly as good. Very clean sound but still ample bass provided that you select the right tip. For me, the standard tip (the one installed as delivered) gave me very little in terms of bass. Selecting a different tip to provide a better ear fit did wonders for bass response.

They are a bit more airy than the RHA sound. That could be a plus or a minus depending on your preferred type of music. Very heavy bass music is not a good match for these. Pretty much everything else is, and I appreciated the enhanced clarity. It’s the type of sound that, when you hear it, the first word that would come to mind is “clean.”

They look odd, make take you a moment to figure out how to position them, but provide a very open, natural sound. It comes with a well-designed kit of useful extras. However, the plug issues, the cord, and the ear loops collectively knock it down a star. Still well worth considering, however, and I would certainly recommend them.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Brainwavz R3 Dual Dynamic Driver Earphones (V2)

Ergonomics:

Canon 2562A002 EF 28-135mm f/3.5-5.6 is USM Standard Zoom Lens for Canon SLR Cameras The Canon 28-135mm f/3.5-5.6 lens with Image Stabilization is a very capable, and more importantly, affordable lens,and is perfect for times when you just want to have one lens on the camera but you also want to have a lot of options with your focal range. While you get the benefits of a slight wide to telephoto range in one handy package, you do lose in light stops as you move through the focal range (the maximum aperture stops down as you move toward the telephoto end of the range). This is where the image stabilization comes in very handy, and allows you to keep hand shake at bay even when you have to compromise on shutter speed to get the correct exposure.

I've had no complaints about the optical quality, I think you'll be pleased with the shots you get from it - the lens may be cheap but don't confuse that with what the quality of image this lens can provide. Keep in mind on a camera with a cropped sensor (any Canon DSLR model other than the 5D and 1D models) the focal range is equivalent to @45-215mm - you lose a bit of the wide angle advantage, but you get more telephoto, so it depends which end of the focal range you value the most as to whether that is a disadvantage or not.
text_fidelity_b: Canon 2562A002 EF 28-135mm f/3.5-5.6 is USM Standard Zoom Lens for Canon SLR Cameras
